column30: Most of those aren't real-world things. Much like junior developers we hire, questions like that are often answered by educating younger developers about the purposes of testing. Most of those checkboxes aren't the purpose. Testing doesn't make *correct*, testing makes *permanent*. Before writing tests it is important to understand the nature of the tests, why you are testing what you are testing, the boundaries of the system under test, and the goals for the suites of tests being added to. There are situations with a strong business case for automated tests, there are situations with a strong business case against automated tests, and it's important to educate the team about which type you're doing on any given project. Automated tests make the most sense when code behavior is permanent, maintained, and shared. Transient systems don't benefit automated testing as the long tail of maintenance doesn't justify the cost, manual testing with thoughtful test plans are cheaper and faster. Unit tests don't test integration, they test the individual unit of code, typically best when you have a verb to perform on data or clear pre/post conditions. Integration tests and feature tests make permanent the bindings between systems, they are critical in long-term supported code but are a waste of time on once-and-done or once-and-iterated gameplay code. Tests integrated into build systems, integrated into version control, integrated into pre-checkin tools, integrated into editors, all of them have their place. There are tests as specification, tests as documentation, test as safety nets.

column41:
In gamedev, most of "everyday" code is *very* fuzzy or very ingrained with the rest of the game/engine which complicates making tests for.
Like, every now and then we have code which deals with a "missing reference" in Unity.
How would we test that given that these code usually depends on (potentially deep) hierarchies of GameObjects existing?
Also, lets say 95% of all code potentially has this issue (basically every Monobehaviour/ScriptableObject).
Even if we suppose it was practical to exercise all of those codepaths meaningfully, how much time it would take to run tests (constructing GameObject hierarchies takes *a lot* of time in Unity).

There's also something to be said about tests bloating the overall code mass. This then would increase the inertia which makes making changes harder.
Game code and, in particular, gameplay code, are very dynamic in nature. Not only in the sense of reacting to other game objects but also in regards to change (due to design changes, etc) throughout the project.

That all said, what I've found works best are:
- minimize extraordinary codepaths; that is, try to eliminate code branches which need to deal with cases which are rare to happen; "can you refactor your code in such a way that there is no error handling at all?";
- assert code invariants; that is, for example, using `Debug.Assert(conditionWhichWeExpectToAlwaysBeTrueButWereNotCertain);` in strategic places to increase our confidence that our code is dealing with the data we expected it to handle;
- letting the whole team report and quickly react to issues we find while (day-to-day) testing the game, so that when there are errors/issues, we can find them as soon as possible during development; which heavily decreases the chances of shipping errors to players;

Hopefully this all makes sense!

Como QA Lead sênior com mais de 10 anos de experiência em qualidade de software e 6+ anos dedicados exclusivamente à indústria de videogames, participei ativamente do ciclo completo de testes em títulos live-service de alto tráfego, com destaque para a franquia Krunker (Krunker.io Seasons 7, 7.1 e 8, Krunker Strike mobile-optimized e Krunker Royale battle royale), além de projetos em estúdios como Miniclip (Plague Inc., Bowmasters) e FRVR. Minha percepção é que os testes em jogos atuais, especialmente multiplayer FPS e live-service, representam um equilíbrio complexo entre rigor técnico, velocidade de iteração, escalabilidade e foco na experiência emocional do jogador. A qualidade não é apenas ausência de bugs, mas a construção de confiança, retenção e imersão — algo que vai além de requisitos técnicos e exige visão holística.
Práticas atuais observadas nos projetos dos quais participei:

Abordagem híbrida manual + automação: Testes manuais são essenciais para áreas exploratórias, como usabilidade, balance de gameplay, integração de bots/AI e performance em cenários reais (ex: stress tests em modos battle royale com centenas de conexões simultâneas). Automação é aplicada em regressão e CI/CD (com Selenium e Jenkins), liberando tempo para testes criativos. Em Krunker Strike, por exemplo, focamos em otimização de server infrastructure escalável para mobile, garantindo estabilidade em dispositivos variados.
Playtesting como núcleo da qualidade: Sempre priorizei sessões internas e externas para capturar feedback qualitativo sobre diversão, dificuldade e retenção. Em Krunker Royale, identificamos problemas críticos de balance e performance combinando métricas de sessão (tempo de jogo, drop-off points) com observação direta de jogadores.
Integração ágil e cross-functional: Com Scrum e Kanban (certificações CSM, KMP e Flow Manager), o QA é embedded desde o planejamento de sprints. Uso intensivo de JIRA e TestRail para bug tracking, métricas (bug leakage, severity trends, test coverage) e colaboração diária com devs/designers. Isso garante resolução rápida e alinhamento com metas de projeto.
Cross-platform e localization: Testes abrangem web, mobile (iOS/Android), PC e console, com atenção a diferenças de hardware/input. Experiência em localization para o mercado brasileiro (transcreation cultural em Miniclip) reforçou a importância de testes linguísticos e culturais para acessibilidade global.

Desafios e nuances identificados:

Velocidade vs qualidade em live-service: Atualizações frequentes priorizam rapidez, levando a hotfixes reativos. Isso aumenta risco de bugs em produção que afetam retenção (ex: crashes em mobile por otimização insuficiente).
Equipes distribuídas: Comunicação assíncrona em times globais pode atrasar resolução de issues críticos. Mentoring remoto exige esforço extra para manter cultura de continuous improvement.
Limitações da automação: Cobrem funcionalidade, mas não capturam "diversão" ou edge cases imprevisíveis de jogadores reais — o toque humano ainda é insubstituível em gameplay/balance.
Métricas vs intuição: KPIs (defect removal efficiency, coverage >90%) são valiosos, mas a percepção subjetiva do tester experiente detecta issues sutis que dados não revelam.

Sugestões e reflexões para evolução:

Automação inteligente e preditiva: Expandir frameworks para simulação de load multiplayer e integração com analytics in-game, permitindo testes baseados em dados reais de jogadores.
Playtesting estruturado e inclusivo: Incluir early access com comunidades diversas desde alpha, combinando quantitative data (heatmaps, session analytics) com qualitative feedback para reduzir fixes pós-launch.
Shift-left testing: Envolver QA desde design de features, com treinamento cruzado (devs entendendo QA, testers com basics de code) para aceleração.
Cultura sustentável: Evitar burnout com rotação de responsabilidades, feedback 360° e mentoria contínua — equipes mais felizes entregam qualidade superior.
Para estúdios menores: Priorizar ferramentas leves/open-source e processos visuais (Kanban boards) para escalar QA sem burocracia.

Em resumo, acredito que o futuro do QA em games está na fusão de dados/telemetria com IA para testes exploratórios, preservando o elemento humano para o que realmente importa: criar experiências imersivas e justas. Minha trajetória em multiplayer FPS me mostrou que qualidade é arte técnica e emocional. 

Para mais reflexões sobre QA em games, veja meu artigo no LinkedIn Pulse: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/getting-job-series-3-frvr

column41: For the projects I have a say in, I would focus on the utility testing brings to the final product. It can differ significantly based on the team, project stage and scope of the project. The key aspect I prefer to highlight is that testing should increase iteration speed of the day to day work. This is key, because it is easier to get real buy-in from the team, where TDD or testing in general is not commonly practiced. The initiatives to add more testing after the fact tends to focus on reducing regressions or increase confidence in releases (which are very important aspects) but then slows down feature development significantly by making the dev teams daily life harder. Enforcing testing in a project not designed for it is usually quite challenging, especially if it is introduced to a team that has worked without it for a long while. Just as a pragmatic approach, focusing on improving the developer experience and increasing iteration speed, has been a good way for me to introduce testing and get buy-in, which in turn increases testability of the project over time and brings the benefits with it. Just some open thoughts, hope it helps. Sorry for the lack of paragraphs. :)

The biggest challenge I've seen in automated testing for games is keeping test synchronized with the UI / game flow. Time-sensitive operations and dynamic, conditional UI flow are things that constantly break during development. Anytime someone nudge the location of a button, or introduces a new pop-up, or login takes longer due to more game data needing to be delivered by the server, or there's network latency it breaks integration tests, or produces a false failure.

Unit testing is much more stable and less prone to false failures, but also offers a lot less value.

I am the primary and sole implementor of the testing/build pipeline at the company I work for. I've advocated for automated testing for a while now, and have finally been given the chance to implement it into our workflows.
As it stands now, whenever a commit is pushed, our code is built as a standalone dll (outside of the engine), and is run through "fast testing," which then publishes the commit status (pending/success/failed) in our VCS. When PRs to the development/release branch are created, integration testing is added on top (in-engine testing), and commits to the development/release branch automatically build and upload the game to a known download location. Notifications are also sent to the team communication channels to inform them of failed integration tests, successful builds, etc. Given approval, I'd love to talk more about the details and how/why I set I up.

Então acho que só vale a pena se o software envolver informações sensíveis como finanças, e/ou se for um projeto grande, que já vai levar muito tempo mesmo. No caso dos jogos a situação piora, porque é muito comum você estar desenvolvendo uma ideia, e de repente mudar o rumo por completo. Isso inviabiliza demais os testes automatizados, porque você teria que ficar sempre reescrevendo, e no fim das contas vai precisar colocar na mão de jogadores reais para testar não só o funcionamento do software, mas outros aspectos como visual, áudio, dificuldade, diversão, etc.
